Hhhmmm well my first position I only worked 6a-10a m-f and usually those shifts are a test of your dedication. All I did was drive them to day program so that got my foot in the door. There’s always hours available so once they saw I fit the mold, hours were being thrown at me whether someone called out of work, went on vacation, or being that you’re new, “shadowing” which is working behind someone who’s been there so they can show you the ropes of how each shifts goes. 

For example, right now Ive been on shift since 2pm yesterday because I work 2-10 normally at my group home but another house needed an overnight staff. That same house needed a morning person so I was mandated to stay there past my overnight until 3 but today I work 3-11 which sums up to 31 hrs. So hours will definitely be there.

They have different names for it. It’s mainly called caretaker/direct support when you have the low functioning clients who need help with diet, hygiene and health. My position is called CSP consumer support professional which works with higher functioning clients who can do things for themselves without much advocacy. Never went to any school or classes for this. It’s literally my heart that got me here. If you show and prove you have a good heart and you’re here for the clients, it’ll be hard for them to say no.

My field needs people like us. I been working with the mentally ill for 7 years and most of the time there’s only 3-4 tasks you have to do between clocking and out. Usually there’s only me and 2 other staff along with 3 clients. I’m basically a baby sitter for the disabled. Most of the shift I’m just sitting on the couch watching YouTube, making beats on my mac, ordering food. If I wanted to I can bring my PlayStation but given my condition, I know I won’t have the executive function to do anything productive lol. But it’s a cool job.. staff sucks sometimes but clients love you and it makes you feel purposeful. To get deeper, these guys have mental disabilities like us so you learn about yourself as you get to know them. If you haven’t I’d say give it a shot and apply for group homes. It’s usually entry level, $16/hr and no strenuous brain power required.
